Existing 3D understanding approaches, however, require captured multi-view scenes, have limited generalization capabilities, or rely on expensive per-scene processing and optimization. To bridge this gap, our method distills complementary knowledge from a camera-controlled video diffusion model and frozen 2D vision foundation models into a unified model to jointly infer 3D Gaussians encoding geometry, appearance, open-vocabulary semantics, and class-agnostic instance cues. The resulting scenes support novel-view rendering, open-vocabulary segmentation, and object grouping without per-scene optimization, while training requires neither manual 3D annotations nor captured multi-view data. Our method outperforms baselines combining state-of-the-art 3DGS segmentation approaches with generative 3D scene reconstruction on curated synthetic and real-image-conditioned benchmarks, while preserving reconstruction quality. Furthermore, our latent formulation naturally extends to monocular video, reconstructing structured dynamic 3D scenes across time. By turning renderable but unstructured outputs into queryable 3D worlds, LucidLyra enables downstream applications including 3D scene editing, 3D asset mining, and robotic simulation.

physical.title: IMPACT: Inverter-Informed Multimodal Learning for Photovoltaic Generation Forecasting
physical.summary: This work develops a physics-informed multimodal deep learning framework for 10- to 110-minute-ahead probabilistic photovoltaic power forecasting. The forecasting model is built on a four-branch architecture that separately encodes plant-level temporal history and inverter-level spatial cloud dynamics through a graph attention encoder with a learned adjacency, known-future solar geometry, and the current meteorological state, fused through gated cross-attention. The geometry branch adds two forward-looking physical signals, spatial cloud heterogeneity and inverter ramp-down activity, each empirically weighted toward the horizon where it is most predictive. The decoder anchors its prediction to a smart persistence baseline, learning a horizon-conditioned correction, and the resulting quantile forecasts are calibrated online through a kernel-weighted adaptive conformal calibration step. The proposed model outperforms all 14 baselines, achieving a forecast skill score (FSS) of 0.2950, 0.099 above the next-best model. A branch-composition ablation shows that every branch contributes positively and the model retains substantial skill in challenging overcast and variable sky conditions (FSS 0.198 and 0.255).

physical.title: Causal-prior-constrained deep learning for rapid-intensification warning of western North Pacific tropical cyclones
physical.summary: Rapid intensification (RI) is one of the most dangerous and unpredictable phases of tropical cyclones, and its environmental and structural drivers are difficult to identify and separate in observations. Here we introduce CausalVisionRI, a causal-prior-constrained deep-learning system for 24-h RI warning in the western North Pacific. It integrates infrared remote sensing imagery, atmospheric and oceanic fields, and an observationally discovered causal graph into a unified model. The graph and eight sign-verified effects on 24-h intensity change provide an auditable causal prior for training. Discovered from 522 cyclones in 2000-2017, it identifies causal pathways linking atmospheric and oceanic conditions, the cyclone's dynamical and structural state, and its 24-h intensity change. On a forward holdout covering 2020-2024 and 3,004 records, the five-member ensemble achieves a Brier skill score (BSS) of 0.259 relative to a fixed development climatology, significantly exceeding four reference systems; the three LDA baselines reach at most 0.105. It also attains higher detection rates than a published knowledge-block scheme and a reconstructed contrastive-learning scheme at matched false-detection rates under our USA 30-kt standard and the published RITCF standard. Ablations show that the graph pathway adds 0.032 BSS across the holdout and 0.063 over 2020-2021, with a significant contribution in one ensemble member. A deep-learning model constrained by observationally discovered causal structure thus offers a new route to physically informed RI warning.

physical.title: RoboAtom: Large-scale Atomic-Action Supervision for Robot Learning
physical.summary: Fine-grained action annotations can support skill reuse and compositional generalization in robot policies. However, robot datasets typically provide task-level instructions without subtask annotations. Although some include subtask labels, inconsistent formats and conventions hinder cross-source joint training. We propose RoboAtom-Data, which adds unified, time-aligned atomic-action annotations to existing data from multiple sources, covering 1.45 million trajectories, 6.88 million skill-labeled segments, and 16,882.1 hours. Our pipeline combines a unified protocol, large-scale manual annotation, propagation across repeated executions with the same ordered skill sequence, and multi-stage quality control. We evaluate the dataset through automatic atomic-action annotation and robot control. We construct RoboAtom-Bench to standardize evaluation of skill recognition and temporal boundary localization. Trained on the annotated data, RoboAtom-Anno achieves better automatic annotation performance than all evaluated open- and closed-source models on both RoboAtom-Bench and the external WGO-Bench. For robot control, atomic-action supervision paired with hierarchical execution improves task success over task-level baselines on LIBERO-Long, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin. We will release the data, benchmark, model, and construction pipeline to support further research on skill-level robot learning.

physical.title: A physics-informed uncertainty-aware surrogate for $p$-$n$ junction diodes
physical.summary: We develop an uncertainty-aware physics-informed surrogate for a one-dimensional $p$-$n$ junction diode, conditioned on device length, doping and bias. Using the internal state of the device as predicted by the surrogate we develop a test-suite of quantities of interest including the terminal current, depletion width, peak field and stored charge. The formalism and the quantities are can be extended to asymmetric junction and two-dimensional diodes as shown by means of benchmark analysis. For the one-dimensional symmetric junction surrogate, we obtain 0.11% median $L_1$ error on the electrostatic potential, and 1.5% and 0.61% on the electron and hole densities. Finally, we develop an uncertainty analysis which determines the validity of surrogate answer within the user-specified tolerance.

physical.title: UniffordInteractor: Reasoning the Unified Affordance for Human and Multi-Object Interaction
physical.summary: Deriving plausible and dynamic Human Object Interaction (HOI) has gained tremendous progress in Embodied AI and Immersive AR/VR. While existing HOI methods have effectively explored human interaction with individual or fixed objects, they still show limitations in complex multi-object interaction scenes. Meanwhile, previous approaches focus more on the contact information held by human-object relation, overlooking the significance of the contact situation of various entities (i.e., object-object). To address these limitations, we propose UniffordInteractor, a Reasoning-then-Interacting framework that leverages unified affordance for realistic and long-horizon human and multi-object interaction modeling. At the reasoning stage, we devise a Unified Affordance Reasoner (UAR) that employs a fine-tuned 3D Multimodal Large Language Model for unified object-centric affordance prediction. At the interacting stage, we propose Hierarchical Interaction Generator (HIG), which formulates the interaction generation as a hierarchical (e.g., root to body to hand to objects) autoregressive prediction, conditioned on the obtained unified affordance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that UniffordInteractor surpasses SOTA counterparts in human and multi-object interaction generation.

physical.title: PairWatch: Pair-Aware Anomaly Transformer for Detecting Adversarial Rendezvous in Public Satellite Catalogs
physical.summary: Documented adversarial rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) appear in the public TLE catalog, yet existing TLE-based maneuver detectors treat each satellite in isolation - mistaking routine station-keeping for adversarial behavior and missing RPO entirely when the target stays passive. We argue that the right unit is the satellite pair and the right inductive bias is the kinematic symmetry between approach and recede. We instantiate both with PairWatch, a pair-aware AnomalyTransformer whose attention prior is augmented with a sign-symmetric geometric similarity over relative-motion features, and release an open benchmark of 359 windows from public Space-Track data spanning 11 documented RPO events, 100 Clohessy-Wiltshire synthetic adversarial windows, and a five-class hard-negative set culminating in the TerraSAR-X / TanDEM-X helix formation. Under the deployment-relevant criterion of a single threshold separating real RPO from operational negatives - a necessary property for catalog-scale screening - PairWatch is the only model that succeeds, with the property holding in 100% of bootstrap resamples versus 0-19.5% for three neural baselines and under 0.1% for four physics-informed detectors. A per-source analysis exposes a shortcut-learning failure mode of single-number AUROC: simpler baselines attain higher overall AUROC by shortcutting a synthetic-vs-formation contrast with no operational meaning; removing this single cell flips the test ranking entirely (LSTM-AD), and these baselines fail the security-relevant task the benchmark was built to measure.

physical.title: UMI-Live for In-The-Wild Bimanual Robotics Data Collection
physical.summary: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. We design our custom UMI-Live hardware to integrate camera and LiDAR--inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power, without external tracking equipment or calibration within the collection environment. We implement a simple user interface for recording data while an asynchronous pipeline performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. We also release software that supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference. We validate UMI-Live data quality by fine-tuning $π_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10, respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. Furthermore, we release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks, and complete hardware designs, software, and reproduction guides at our $\href{https://umi-live.github.io/}{\text{project website}}$.

physical.title: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh: GPU-Native Meshes and Simulation Cases for Physics AI
physical.summary: PhysicsNeMo-Mesh is the mesh module of the open-source PhysicsNeMo library. It provides mesh processing similar to PyVista, but on the GPU, in batches, and inside PyTorch's automatic differentiation. Like xarray for unstructured meshes, it attaches semantics to data: fields on points, cells, and whole meshes have names and shapes, and a simulation case keeps the complete PDE problem specification, including boundary conditions and their prescribed values. It addresses three problems that plague machine learning for physical simulation. First, GPU utilization is bottlenecked by I/O, because samples are very large relative to the compute per forward pass. Second, because traditional preprocessing is expensive, it is necessarily done once, during curation, rather than differently for each model and workflow at the point of use. Finally, advanced equivariant and mesh-native architectures require information that curation ordinarily discards. Fast GPU mesh processing makes it practical to preprocess at the point of use: on one GB200 GPU, mesh operations run $6.2\text{--}1{,}068\times$ faster than VTK with 72 threads, and loading a whole case is $8.0\text{--}88\times$ faster than reading its VTK files ($8.0\times$ when both read the same fields). Overlapped with training, this preprocessing costs $2.1\%$ of throughput for a $127\,\text{ms}$ Transolver step. So one dataset serves many models and workflows: in PhysicsNeMo's public recipe, one stored DrivAerML dataset feeds Transolver, GeoTransolver, and GLOBE. PhysicsNeMo-Mesh combines the speed of an intermediate array store with the flexibility of an archival format such as VTK. When shapes and wall conditions both vary, per-boundary conditions cut a heat-conduction error from $87\%$ to $6\text{--}9\%$. And by keeping field ranks and named boundaries, it retains the semantic structure that next-generation architectures will need.

physical.title: Robotic Data Inoculation
physical.summary: Modern robot learning systems feed on high-quality demonstration data, and their performance hinges on coverage. Without good coverage, small errors compound and the policy can quickly go into out-of-distribution states from which it cannot recover. Yet there is no principled way of collecting high-coverage data, and data collection often relies on heuristic instructions to human operators. Purely online reinforcement learning (RL) explores at the cost of safety and sample efficiency, while DAgger-style interventions require the policy to fail by chance before a human can correct it. In this paper, we ask instead whether we can modify how the robot behaves during data collection to collect more useful data. We propose Data Inoculation (DI), a shared-control framework in which a human provide closed-loop teleoperation commands while a residual policy perturbs these commands. The residual policy is trained online, on the growing dataset, with the same reward-maximizing objective later used for policy extraction, so its perturbations steer data collection toward the deviations a policy trained on the data would make. These perturbations expose the robot to a wider range of states, while the human's continuous corrections provide recovery demonstrations, "inoculating" the dataset against the learner's future mistakes while the human remains in control. On three challenging real-world robotic tasks, DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of policies trained with both behavioral cloning and offline RL, showing DI as an effective data collection strategy for improving downstream policy performance.

physical.title: The Utility of Physics-Informed Machine Learning in Solar Power Production Forecasting
physical.summary: Physics-informed machine learning (PIML) and hybrid modeling have attracted significant attention as approaches for combining physical knowledge with the flexibility of deep learning. In this work, we investigate whether these approaches deliver their commonly claimed benefits for large-scale photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting. We develop two hybrid forecasting architectures that integrate the ADR physical PV efficiency model with the TSMixer neural forecasting architecture through feature augmentation and residual learning. The proposed models are evaluated on a dataset comprising over 3 million samples from 3,713 PV installations across 33 European countries. We assess convergence speed, forecasting accuracy, transferability across geographical regions, and data efficiency. Although the physics-informed models seem to exhibit slightly faster convergence during training, they do not achieve consistent improvements in test-set accuracy, generalization, or performance under limited training data compared to the purely data-driven baseline. These findings suggest that, for modern deep forecasting architectures trained on large datasets, explicitly incorporating the ADR physical model provides limited practical benefit for day-ahead PV forecasting.

physical.title: Inherent Failure Modes of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Buoyancy-Driven Flow: Role of Non-Dimensionalization in Network Training
physical.summary: We investigate the influence of non-dimensionalization on the trainability and accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for buoyancy-driven flows. Using a differentially heated square cavity at $\mathrm{Pr}=0.71$ and $\mathrm{Ra}=10^3$--$10^5$, we compare thermal-diffusive and free-fall velocity scalings under identical training conditions. The free-fall scaling, with a unit buoyancy coefficient, achieves errors below 1.1\% in the mean Nusselt number for $\mathrm{Ra}\le10^4$, whereas the diffusive scaling, with a buoyancy coefficient of $\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr}$, produces errors of 157--650\% and diverges at $\mathrm{Ra}=10^5$. We identify a coefficient-induced gradient imbalance, with the dominant buoyancy-related contribution to the loss gradient scaling as $(\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr})^2$, and confirm it through direct gradient measurements. Neither sparse-data supervision nor adaptive loss weighting resolves the training difficulties under the tested conditions. For unsteady convection, the free-fall PINN accurately predicts long-time heat transfer but fails to capture the transient Nusselt-number overshoot. These findings establish non-dimensionalization as an important design consideration for improving PINN trainability in buoyancy-driven flows.

physical.title: UnEZ: A Fully Unsupervised Self-Templating Neural Network for Redshift and Line Strength Estimation
physical.summary: As spectroscopic surveys grow, estimating galaxy properties such as metallicity, star formation rate, and redshift becomes computationally cumbersome. Methods of estimating such properties rely on template spectra or curated redshift catalogs, which fail to represent the diversity of objects seen in large-scale surveys. We present UnEZ, a fully unsupervised, physics-informed machine learning model that can predict spectroscopic redshifts and line strengths with no prior redshift or line strength labels. An encoder predicts emission and absorption line amplitudes/widths, and a fixed deterministic decoder constructs a unique template, estimated redshift, redshift confidence curve, and spectral model. UnEZ was tested on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) Data Release 18 due to its large dataset and thoroughly vetted redshift catalog which serves as an independent benchmark. Despite the lack of templates, line strength labels, or redshift labels, UnEZ's performance competes with modern redshift estimation algorithms. At SNR > 10, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 0.459% and a normalized median absolute deviation (NMAD) of $1.237 \times 10^{-4}$. At SNR > 3, UnEZ achieves an outlier fraction of 3.89% and an NMAD of $1.471 \times 10^{-4}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate how UnEZ's line strength and redshift predictions can be utilized for various purposes such as constructing template spectra required in traditional redshift estimation algorithms. UnEZ illustrates how a fully unsupervised neural network can allow redshift, among other galaxy properties, to emerge naturally from the spectra themselves, providing a template-free, label-free approach that scales to the demands of future surveys.

physical.title: Regional accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for recirculation in a deep lid-driven cavity
physical.summary: Deep lid-driven cavities contain strong motion beneath the lid and much weaker recirculation at depth, so agreement in bulk velocity is an incomplete assessment of a computed flow. We examine data-free physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for steady, two-dimensional incompressible flow in a cavity of depth-to-width ratio five at Reynolds numbers 100, 250, 500 and 1000. An established hard-constrained streamfunction formulation is combined with prescribed regional collocation, transferred initialization, and selected residual-scaling and envelope variants. Independent spectral/$hp$ calculations with the same Gaussian-regularized lid provide the reference fields. For a cavity of depth-to-width ratio $D/W=5$ at Reynolds numbers $\mathrm{Re}=100$, 250, 500, and 1000, evaluation on a common $121\times605$ grid gives interior relative velocity discrepancies of 5.130\%--7.850\%. Over the same cases, floor-region relative velocity discrepancies remain below 5\%, with absolute RMS discrepancies ranging from $1.255\times10^{-10}U$ to $2.332\times10^{-9}U$, where $U$ is the lid-velocity scale. In a separate $161\times801$ assessment at $\Rey=1000$, the refined workflow lowers interior velocity discrepancy from 5.624\% to 2.658\% and gauge-aligned pressure RMS discrepancy from $2.793\times10^{-3}$ to $1.167\times10^{-3}ρU^2$. The improvements compare accumulated training workflows and do not isolate regional sampling. Configuration rankings depend on both region and observable. These finite-budget comparisons establish where the retained workflows agree with the reference and where rotational-field discrepancies remain substantial.

physical.title: Explore Where It Matters: Targeted Exploration for Efficient Rover Adaptation
physical.summary: Future planetary rovers will traverse steep, deformable terrain where slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation can threaten mobility. Although simulation can capture some wheel-soil effects, unmodeled deformable-terrain phenomena create sim-to-real gaps requiring deployment-time adaptation. Yet, rover operations leave little room for extensive trial-and-error. We introduce TERRA (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation), an online adaptation framework that efficiently seeks deployment data exposing task-relevant model errors and corrects them. TERRA adapts a simulation-trained world model with a reward-weighted prediction loss and trains a loss predictor to estimate where future performance-relevant errors are likely to occur, using this signal to guide exploration during MPC. In simulation, TERRA reaches approximately 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution pretraining conditions, outperforming exploration baselines in reward, completion time, and energy to first success. On the ERNEST rover, TERRA recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials. Project website: https://terra-explore.github.io

physical.title: pCoRev: Physics-Informed Contrastive Learning for Unsupervised Reverberation Artifact Suppression in Ultrafast Plane-Wave Imaging
physical.summary: Reverberation artifact suppression in ultrafast plane-wave (PW) imaging remains challenging because artifact-free reference data are generally unavailable and multipath echoes often resemble tissue signals. Coherent plane-wave compounding (CPWC) attenuates reverberation only partially and sacrifices the frame rate that motivates PW imaging. We propose pCoRev, an unsupervised physics-informed contrastive learning framework that leverages the distinct angular coherence characteristics of tissue echoes and reverberation artifacts. A single-angle I/Q frame is the network input, and the remaining angles of the same CPWC acquisition provide angle-consistent positive pairs, residual-derived negative pairs, and coherence-guided self-supervision, so no paired artifact-free data are required. On a fabricated reverberation phantom with 31 validation acquisitions, pCoRev achieved the best contrast ratio (CR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and generalized CNR (gCNR) of 38.76 +/- 5.40 dB, 11.75 +/- 1.81 dB, and 0.932 +/- 0.051 against delay-and-sum (DAS), delay-multiply-and-sum, a supervised 3D convolutional neural network, and unsupervised deep coherence learning. Because the network is trained on single-angle inputs, it also operates on a single PW transmission: with one angle, pCoRev reached a CR of 32.10 +/- 7.79 dB and a CNR of 10.39 +/- 3.02 dB, exceeding 75-angle compounded DAS (20.45 +/- 3.84 dB and 8.38 +/- 2.00 dB) with 75-fold fewer transmissions. On four clinical acquisitions from other scanners, pCoRev improved CR over DAS by 9 to 21 dB without fine-tuning. These results indicate that physics-informed unsupervised contrastive learning suppresses reverberation effectively while preserving the frame-rate advantage of ultrafast PW imaging.

physical.title: A Hybrid Physics-informed holomorphic neural networks Method
physical.summary: Physics-informed holomorphic neural networks (PIHNNs) exploit complex-analytic representations to satisfy homogeneous PDEs by construction, but their extension to nonhomogeneous problems is nontrivial. We propose a hybrid physics-informed holomorphic neural network (HPIHNN) framework based on a decomposition of the solution into particular and homogeneous components. The particular component is computed by a spectral method on a simple extended domain, while the homogeneous component is approximated by a PIHNN trained only on the boundary with modified boundary data. The resulting formulation avoids meshing complex geometries and retains the dimensionality-reduction advantage of holomorphic representations. The method is applied to nonhomogeneous Poisson, Stokes, biharmonic, linear elasticity, and Helmholtz equations. Numerical experiments covering complex geometries, corner singularities, and nearly incompressible regimes demonstrate that the proposed method accurately resolves the corresponding solutions and, in the considered tests, generally achieves lower errors and shorter training times than standard PINNs. The results indicate that coupling spectral particular solutions with holomorphic neural approximations provides an efficient approach to nonhomogeneous PDEs on complex domains.

physical.title: Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Evaluation
physical.summary: Embodied systems can update policies, world models, skills, and executable programs from deployment experience, allowing one interaction to benefit later tasks. When a system also revises and reuses its data-acquisition, feedback, or learning procedures, experience changes the process that produces capability, introducing recursive self-improvement. This paper surveys research in physical AI through the connection between persistent capability and its improvement process. We first explain the functional distinction between learner updates and improvers, then compare policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable harnesses. These approaches connect to revisions of curricula, rewards, and research programs in different ways. Contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs determine whether the resulting gains accumulate during continued deployment. An L0-L3 rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. Representative benchmarks and within-study contrasts relate these distinctions to existing results. We further propose common-data and interactive comparisons that evaluate reference and revised improvers from shared learner starts, separating the use of experience from its acquisition. This perspective connects the diverse methods, physical operating conditions, and evaluation evidence, underpinning embodied RSI. A comprehensive list of studies in this survey is available at https://github.com/nkd-lkz/physical-ai-rsi-survey.

physical.title: A Physics-Informed Neural Network for Geodesic Computation and Visualization of Geodesic Spheres on Riemannian Manifolds
physical.summary: Visualizing geodesic structures associated with general Riemannian metrics is a challenging problem in computational differential geometry. In this work, we present a computational framework for visualizing geodesics and geodesic spheres on a three-dimensional Riemannian manifold equipped with the metric $g=\text{diag}(1,x^2,1), x>0$. The associated Christoffel symbols and curvature tensors are computed symbolically, and the resulting geodesic equations are solved using both \texttt{SciPy}'s numerical integration method and a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN). The two solutions are compared to assess the accuracy of the neural network approximation. We further develop geodesic spike diagrams and surface visualizations to illustrate the deformation of geodesic spheres relative to their Euclidean counterparts. Intrinsic Riemannian surface area and volume are estimated numerically using the induced metric and the Riemannian volume density, respectively. For the chosen metric and a geodesic ball of radius one, the computed area and volume are approximately $0.362\%$ and $0.364\%$ smaller than the corresponding Euclidean values at the base grid resolution. A grid-refinement study is also performed to examine the sensitivity of these estimates to numerical resolution. The proposed framework demonstrates how symbolic differential geometry, numerical integration, and PINNs can be combined to investigate and visualize geometric structures associated with Riemannian metrics.

physical.title: Crystoria: A Large-Scale Crystal Dataset Linking Thermodynamic and Dynamical Stability for Materials AI
physical.summary: Large-scale crystal databases have transformed materials discovery by making millions of structures and thermodynamic properties accessible to materials informatics. Yet dynamical stability remains sparsely characterized at a comparable scale because its evaluation is substantially more computationally demanding than conventional structure and energy calculations. This mismatch creates a critical gap between the rapidly expanding crystal-structure space and the physical information available for materials research and machine learning. Here we introduce Crystoria, a large-scale crystal dataset designed to bring dynamical stability to the scale of modern materials data. We construct Crystoria by systematically curating low-energy and metastable inorganic crystals, standardizing their structural identities, and combining machine-learning-accelerated structural relaxation with phonon-based dynamical screening. The resulting dataset contains 2,649,640 crystal structures, spanning 89 elements, 219 of the 230 space groups, and primitive cells containing 1-48 atoms. Among them, 1,793,353 structures (67.68%) are classified as dynamically stable, revealing substantial variation in dynamical stability across chemical and crystallographic space. By bringing dynamical stability to the scale of millions of crystal structures, Crystoria provides a physically grounded foundation for materials artificial intelligence (AI) and enables systematic exploration of the dynamical crystal landscape.

physical.title: Same Label, Different Interface: Beyond Action-Space Labels in Robot Learning
physical.summary: Robot-learning studies often compare position and velocity actions as though each label identified a single experimental treatment, yet the label alone does not determine what the robot executes. Before affecting robot motion, bounded policy output passes through filtering, physical scaling, reference construction, feedback, timing, and effort limits. We study how these omitted properties affect attribution under one shared learner and training budget. Across three contact-rich Factory tasks (PegInsert, GearMesh, and NutThread), we compare five joint-space interfaces, with ten independently trained policies per condition. We first remain within the same position-feedback law and vary the executed interface: substituting only the physical action scale as the directly modified component changes sample-median evaluation success by 0.645-1.000 across tasks, while removing an exponential moving average produces task-dependent changes. We then move to a cross-law comparison and choose a velocity scale that exactly matches the position interface's local raw-torque command gain. This calibration raises the sample median on GearMesh and NutThread, with no median change on PegInsert. Yet clear residual sample-median gaps remain on PegInsert and GearMesh, while the NutThread interval includes zero. Thus, even this explicit equality leaves feedback and held-action dynamics unmatched and does not establish position-velocity trained-outcome equivalence. Action-interface comparisons should therefore report the executed pathway and state the physical quantity they match.

physical.title: Neural Stream Function Method for Electrical Impedance Tomography with Lipschitz Conductivities
physical.summary: Electrical impedance tomography (EIT) reconstructs the conductivity inside an object from voltage and current measurements on its boundary. The resulting inverse problem is nonlinear and severely ill-posed. Neural networks offer a flexible computational approach, but training physics informed neural networks for EIT and relating their training loss to reconstruction accuracy remain challenging. We develop a novel constrained neural stream function method for planar EIT with Lipschitz conductivities. The method builds the conductivity constraints and prescribed boundary voltages into the neural trial functions and replaces the second order conductivity equation with a first order system in strong form. The measured current is also used to construct a fixed baseline for the stream function. For this formulation, we derive error estimates that relate the sampled neural objective to errors in the physical boundary currents and the reconstructed conductivity. The error estimates separate the contributions from neural approximation, measurement noise, and sampling. Numerical experiments further demonstrate that the proposed method achieves high reconstruction accuracy with both exact and noisy boundary data.

physical.title: Where the Error Lives: Spectral Representations of Learned Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians
physical.summary: Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) is the standard method for computing the electronic structure of molecules and materials, but its self-consistent-field (SCF) iterations make it expensive for large systems and high-throughput screening. Machine-learned Hamiltonian models offer a shortcut: an equivariant network predicts the Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian matrix in one forward pass, and diagonalizing the prediction yields orbital energies, the HOMO-LUMO gap, molecular orbitals and the electron density. These models are trained to match the reference matrix entry by entry, yet a small entry-wise error does not guarantee accurate eigenvalues or eigenvectors. Two physics-informed alternatives go partway: a recently proposed wavefunction-alignment loss adds a spectral penalty without diagonalizing the prediction, and matching the electron density of the diagonalized prediction supervises it directly. Neither is complete: by representing the prediction error in the eigenbasis of the reference Hamiltonian, we show that each sees only part of the error, and that shifting the predicted orbital energies leaves the electron density exactly unchanged. The same analysis identifies a complete training signal: the cumulative local density of states (cumulative LDOS), the number of electrons at each point in space with energy below a given threshold. The cumulative LDOS is a single physical observable that contains the electron density as a special case, responds to every component of the error, determines the Hamiltonian uniquely, and yields gradients that do not vanish for large orbitalenergy errors. Fine-tuning three Hamiltonian networks on QH9 in this way, which we call FermiScope, reduces the HOMO-LUMO gap error without increasing the element-wise error. The gains carry over to out-of-distribution and molecular-dynamics splits, where the wavefunction-alignment loss helps less.

physical.title: Learning Visuomotor Quadrotor Flight Through Dynamic Narrow Gaps via Differentiable Simulation
physical.summary: Threading a quadrotor through a moving narrow gap is a demanding test of agile flight, requiring centimeter-level spatial alignment and precise temporal execution. We address this challenge using a control policy that operates directly on onboard visual and inertial measurements to output collective thrust and body-rate commands. The task is difficult because success lies on a thin feasible manifold: small errors in timing, position, attitude, or visual observability cause collision. Prior planning and learning methods rely on privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation; learning dynamic narrow-gap traversal directly, from scratch, remains open. We introduce a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane, turning a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective. We integrate this formulation into a visual-feature-to-command policy trained in one stage from random initialization, without a teacher, planner, or distillation. We validate our approach in both synthetic and real-world experiments. In controlled benchmarks, we demonstrate that pathwise gradients significantly outperform score-function gradients for precision-critical tasks, yielding a 99.3% success rate in simulation after only a few minutes of training on a single GPU. Furthermore, the policy transfers directly to a real quadrotor, successfully crossing a dynamic narrow gap from varied initial conditions using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an 80% success rate over 10 physical trials.

physical.title: QD-PINN:A Physics-Informed Neural Network Approach to Bayesian Quickest Detection in High-Dimensional Diffusions
physical.summary: Quickest detection problems (QDPs) arise in a wide range of applications. However, the complementarity structure of the associated variational inequalities poses substantial challenges for traditional numerical methods, particularly in high-dimensional settings. We propose a PINN-based framework for estimating the optimal stopping boundary in QDPs with high-dimensional diffusion processes and spatial dependence, while overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Theoretically, we establish a novel equivalence between the free-boundary PDE and an infinite-dimensional stochastic optimization problem, rigorously justifying the use of finite-dimensional neural networks to approximate the true solution. Furthermore, we assess the robustness of the proposed framework by quantifying uncertainty in the learned stopping boundaries using deep ensembles and Monte Carlo dropout. The results show low variability across independent training runs and stochastic forward passes, indicating stable and consistent boundary estimates. We also compare our PINN results with reference numerical solutions where available and find close agreement.

physical.title: Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception
physical.summary: Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence. In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly. Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer. Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves. To strengthen this capability, we propose EvidenceConnect, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence. To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions. We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2). Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning. These results establish EvidenceConnect as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.

physical.title: A Deep Learning-Driven Operator Splitting Scheme for Free Boundary Problems: An Application to American Option Pricing in Incomplete Markets
physical.summary: This paper proposes a deep learning-driven operator splitting scheme for high-dimensional free-boundary problems, with American option pricing as a representative application. In a market with proportional transaction costs, a stochastic liquidity risk with an empirically validated nonlinear drift based on S&P 500 data, and two-factor stochastic volatility, the pricing problem takes the form of a five-dimensional highly nonlinear variational inequality. The proposed scheme decomposes this variational inequality at each time layer into an elliptic continuation equation approximated by a physics-informed neural network and a closed-form projection step enforcing the early-exercise constraint. A conditional $\ell^\infty$ stability bound is derived under stated resolvent and Lipschitz assumptions. The scheme is validated against finite-difference and least-squares Monte Carlo benchmarks, and both the option prices and the learned exercise boundary show close agreement with the reference solutions. Sensitivity analyses with respect to the key model parameters are also reported.

physical.title: Stiffness coefficients in granular micromechanics determined with three-point bending experiments and digital image correlation for a bimodulus material
physical.summary: This study presents an inverse analysis to determine the stiffness parameters of a bimodulus constitutive model formulated within a granular micromechanics framework. Full-field normal strain measurements are obtained by Digital Image Correlation (DIC) during three-point bending tests and are used as experimental input to a hybrid numerical optimization procedure. The experimental campaign is designed to ensure that the measured strain fields remain within the elastic regime. Since the identification is formulated as a nonlinear regression problem, a physically informed initial parameter set is constructed to guide the optimization toward mechanically meaningful values. An initial estimate of the compressive stiffness is first obtained from the available manufacturer data. The tension-compression stiffness asymmetry is then estimated from the experimentally measured neutral-axis shift, which provides a macroscopic signature of bimodulus material behavior in bending. These estimates define the initial parameter set, which is subsequently refined through a hybrid optimization procedure based on the full-field comparison of the experimental and numerical normal strain distributions. The identified parameter set enables the numerical model to reproduce more closely both the through-depth profile and the spatial distribution of the normal strain component over the selected surface region. These results demonstrate that full-field normal strain measurements provide an effective basis for identifying the stiffness parameters of bimodulus granular micromechanics models. The largest differences between the numerical and experimental strain fields are observed near the load-application region, where localized strain variations are induced by the concentrated load.

physical.title: When Black-Box Robot Policies Fail: Online Sensor Diagnosis and Repair with a Transparent Surrogate
physical.summary: Robot foundation models may generalize across tasks and embodiments, but their actions still depend on sensors that can fail. When the policy is frozen or inaccessible, can an external monitor diagnose and repair corrupted inputs without access to its internals? We test a structured surrogate that separates periodic gait from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair around a frozen locomotion policy. On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis raises walking success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reaches 382/640, with no triggers in 64 held-out fault-free episodes. A matched boosted-tree surrogate predicts clean actions similarly well but yields no detected repair improvement over no repair. Separate fits improve walking on Go1 and ANYmal C, although phase-aware gradients perform better. Evidence remains limited to one policy and a partly screened simulated fault suite; robot foundation model and hardware validation remain open.

physical.title: Machine Learning Hamiltonians with Polarizations for Heterogeneous Systems
physical.summary: Machine learning Hamiltonians use local atomic structures to determine local Hamiltonian matrix elements without carrying out self-consistent calculations. They have been used to study large systems and to carry out high-throughput screening for their electronic and optical properties. The prediction of the Hamiltonian is essentially the prediction of the electron electrostatic potential energy; however, for heterogeneous systems, this potential energy is often determined by faraway features, such as interface or surface dipoles, or even an applied voltage in a nanodevice. Thus, it cannot be determined by local atomic structures alone. In this sense, one needs to solve the electron electrostatic potential energy self-consistently using intrinsic atomic dipoles, the applied external potential energy, and polarizabilities. Fortunately, the intrinsic dipoles and polarizabilities are local properties, whereas the applied potential energy is a prescribed input. In this work, we propose DeepH-Polar, a physically informed machine learning Hamiltonian model that explicitly predicts intrinsic atomic dipoles and polarizability tensors and uses them to solve the electron electrostatic potential energy self-consistently. Benchmarks on polar GaN systems and crystalline-Si/amorphous-SiO$_2$ interfaces demonstrate improved Hamiltonian accuracy and reproduction of thickness-dependent electrostatic variations, as well as spatially nonuniform field-induced screening that models without polarization fail to capture. Our model also allows us to study nanoscale electronic devices. By iteratively solving the Hamiltonian eigenproblem and self-consistently updating free-carrier occupations and the electrostatic potential, we simulate an 8,194-atom gated semiconductor device.

physical.title: TAPESTRY: A Single Backbone for Video Generation and Robot Control
physical.summary: Pretrained video generation models encode rich priors about physical interactions, but leveraging them for robot control typically requires either resource-intensive video generation at test time or action heads trained from scratch that do not fully utilize the pretrained backbone. We introduce Tokenizing Actions as Video Patches in a Shared Transformer Policy (TAPESTRY), a world action model that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer into a robotic policy without requiring video generation at inference. Our key idea is to treat robot actions as single-patch tokens in the video model's latent space. A lightweight linear projection maps each action timestep to the patch dimensions of the pretrained VAE, and the resulting tokens are processed by the same patchifying layers and transformer backbone used for video. The shared backbone is optimized through three diffusion objectives sampled per minibatch element: Video diffusion uses VAE latents from robot and human videos to establish dynamics priors. Joint video+action diffusion trains on robot demonstrations using a coupled diffusion timestep and an asymmetric attention mask. Action-only diffusion denoises actions conditioned on clean image latents. At test time, the model generates a compact action token sequence in a single DDIM step from pure noise, producing smooth action chunks at 84 ms per action chunk on consumer hardware and avoiding the cost of full video generation. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot experiments, TAPESTRY achieves strong performance with substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video--action policies. More information can be found at https://tapestry-wam.github.io.

physical.title: Rethinking Channel Estimation for Fluid Antenna Systems: A Physics-Informed Operator Learning
physical.summary: Fluid antenna systems (FAS) leverage continuous reconfigurable apertures to transcend the spatial limits of fixed-position arrays, yet acquiring full-aperture channel state information (CSI) from sparse observations remains a formidable bottleneck. In this paper, we establish a continuous-field formulation for FAS by recasting channel estimation as a stochastic inverse field-reconstruction problem constrained by the projected Helmholtz model. Through electromagnetic information theory (EIT)-based spectral leakage analysis, we demonstrate that finite-aperture reconstruction induces an intrinsic convolutional relationship in the spectral domain, rendering the estimation task a fundamental frequency-domain inverse deconvolution problem. To solve this, we propose a U-shaped Fourier neural operator (UFNO) specifically tailored for noisy, underdetermined wireless environments. Furthermore, we leverage the Landau--Pollak theorem to derive an aperture-dependent EDoF bound that guides the spatial mode budget, and employ a physics-aware Sobolev loss to promote consistency in both channel values and spatial variations. Unlike conventional learning-based approaches, a single frozen UFNO can be directly evaluated at unseen spatial--frequency resolutions without resolution-specific retraining or explicit output interpolation. Extensive simulations show that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks in accuracy while achieving orders-of-magnitude lower inference latency than iterative solvers at high spatial--frequency resolutions.

physical.title: RoboSTD: Zero-Shot Single-to-Dual Transfer via Sagittal Mirroring for Bimanual Learning
physical.summary: Bimanual robot manipulation plays an important role in real-world robotic applications, but the high cost of collecting bimanual demonstrations limits the scalable development of bimanual policy learning. Meanwhile, existing single-arm manipulation data are difficult to directly transfer to bimanual systems due to the Single-to-Dual gap in action spaces, coordination requirements, and arm-side spatial preference. To address this issue, we propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot Single-to-Dual data construction method for bimanual robot learning. RoboSTD first applies sagittal-plane mirroring to observations, proprioception, and actions to construct executable contralateral pseudo-demonstrations. It then uses an LLM to generate structured spatio-temporal coordination constraints that guide the reconstruction of pseudo-bimanual supervision across workspace regions and task stages. We evaluate RoboSTD on the AgileX ALOHA platform in both RoboTwin simulation and real-world settings. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RoboSTD for bimanual policy learning. Without requiring additional bimanual demonstrations, RoboSTD increases the average number of collected cups to 2.11x that of the single-arm baseline in the cup collection task. Project page: https://huahungy.github.io/RoboSTD/

physical.title: From Biological Curves to Soft Modular Robots: Learning-Based Inverse Design with Uncertainty-Guided Refinement
physical.summary: Animals exhibit diverse shape-changing behaviors, from the undulatory swimming of eels to the arching movements of inchworms. Reproducing these biological shapes with modular soft robots offers a promising approach to developing versatile bioinspired robotic systems. However, translating a desired shape into a feasible robotic configuration remains challenging. Existing cable-driven modular soft robots rely on computationally expensive physics-based modeling and combinatorial search for inverse design, making it difficult to efficiently reproduce diverse target shapes. To address this challenge, we present a learning-based real-to-sim-to-real framework that translates biological curves into robotic configurations through surrogate-assisted inverse design and uncertainty-guided refinement. The proposed method combines learned inverse prediction with targeted candidate exploration, using a fast forward surrogate to evaluate and select suitable designs. The learned forward surrogate reduces deformation prediction time from $1.53 \times 10^5$ ms to 0.0008 ms, achieving approximately a $1.9 \times 10^8$-fold speedup. At the same time, the proposed inverse design method reduces design time from $1.99 \times 10^6$ ms to 4.18 ms. On 5,000 test samples generated from previously unseen threading patterns, the method achieves a 93% shape reconstruction success rate under surrogate-based evaluation. Physical demonstrations with four bioinspired robots further illustrate the translation of biological curves into realizable robotic shapes.

physical.title: Learning Multiscale Dynamics of Nanoparticle Self-Assembly
physical.summary: Nanoparticle self-assembly offers a powerful route to programmable functional materials, but its dynamics remain difficult to understand because they arise from multiscale, many-body, and environment-dependent interactions. Liquid-phase transmission electron microscopy (LPTEM) enables real-time observation of these dynamics, yet extracting the underlying physical laws from highly stochastic trajectories remains a significant challenge. Here we develop a physics-informed, time-varying autoregressive framework that learns multiscale self-assembly dynamics directly from LPTEM videos. Continuous Eulerian fields with local density and orientational order are coarse-grained from individual video frames and evolved by a sparse, nearest-neighbor operator optimized over a constrained matrix manifold. This interpretable approach captures long-time large scale phase transitions by tracking operator volatility over time, and short-timescale local evolution and transport rules. Crucially, we extract the underlying partial differential equations, where expected symmetries naturally emerge, enabling the direct inference of fundamental coefficients. Our framework provides a robust, computationally efficient tool for discovering hidden physical mechanisms from observational data, opening a path toward the predictive design of self-assembled nanostructures.

physical.title: SO-101 Bench: Accessible Spatial Manipulation
physical.summary: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.

physical.title: Data-Driven Hamiltonian for Neural Optimal Control
physical.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a prominent data-driven approach to optimal control, but often requires substantial amounts of data and provides limited guarantees when encountering out-of-distribution state-action pairs. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach grounded in the well-established Hamilton-Jacobi framework in optimal control theory. Rather than requiring an explicit analytical model of the system dynamics to evaluate the Hamiltonian, we replace this with a data-driven Hamiltonian (DDH), which we generalize to a broad class of optimal control problems. In contrast to standard RL approaches, the DDH provides a principled mechanism, requiring only minimal prior system information such as a Lipschitz constant, for quantifying and accounting for uncertainty in regions not covered by the data, enabling the derivation of controllers with performance guarantees. Additional prior system knowledge, when available, can be readily incorporated to improve performance. For high-dimensional systems, we further introduce a physics-informed neural approximation of the value function, trained using a novel procedure that generates worst-case fictitious rollouts evaluated through the DDH. On an LQR problem, the DDH reaches near-optimal cost on every dataset we test, including random data on which offline RL methods remain far from optimal, and needs far fewer samples than online RL. On a nonlinear lunar lander benchmark, the DDH achieves an optimality gap to a trajectory-optimization reference more than $3\times$ smaller than CQL and FQL, and matches the performance of SAC with approximately $37\times$ fewer samples. These results establish the DDH as a promising framework for data-driven optimal control, particularly in settings where available data are limited in quantity or quality.

physical.title: ADACT: PDE-Constrained Thermal Hardware/Software Co-Design Adjoint-Driven Optimal Control via Finite Difference Discretization
physical.summary: By virtue of the sheer compute demands of large-scale artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC), modern multi-core microprocessors suffer from severe power density limits and thermal throttling, entailing an urgent need for principled methods for predictive, physics-informed dynamical thermal management (DTM). Here, we introduce a hardware/software co-design physics-informed PDE-constrained DTM throttling optimal control algorithm, ADACT (Adjoint-Driven Adaptive Co-Design Thermal Control), that minimizes thermal risk and cooling energy overhead while maximizing core execution throughput. The underlying physical temperature field is governed by a two-dimensional nonhomogeneous parabolic reaction-diffusion equation with spatially localized, time-varying power source terms and variable convective cooling subject to nonhomogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. We employ a discretization of the continuous state PDE via a Crank-Nicolson finite difference scheme with a 5-point discrete Laplacian operator on a uniform spatial mesh, which preserves unconditional numerical stability and $O(Δx^2 + Δy^2 + Δt^2)$ second-order temporal and spatial accuracy. To efficiently compute exact gradients, we construct and implement a continuous backward-in-time adjoint state method with L-BFGS as our optimization algorithm of choice. The accuracy and second-order convergence rates of both forward state and backward adjoint solvers are quantitatively verified via the Method of Manufactured Solutions (MMS), and gradient accuracy is validated using directional derivative Taylor tests. Numerical experiments demonstrate that ADACT dynamically throttles software power workloads and modulates hardware cooling efforts to strictly uphold physical thermal thresholds while maintaining operational throughput.

physical.title: Multi-Horizon Future Discovery for Physics-Informed Exploration
physical.summary: Exploration in physical control environments requires agents to identify actions whose consequences reveal previously unexplored aspects of the underlying dynamics. However, many intrinsic motivation methods rely on immediate prediction errors, state novelty, or local physical changes, which may overlook informative outcomes that emerge across extended temporal horizons. We investigate whether learning structured representations of reachable futures can provide a more effective basis for exploration. To this end, we introduce Hamiltonian Temporal Contrastive Curiosity (HTC$^2$), a framework that combines multi-horizon temporal representation learning with Hamiltonian phase-space structure. A horizon-conditioned contrastive critic learns temporal relationships from future-state pairs sampled within the same episode. The distance between positive-pair representations is then used as an intrinsic reward, encouraging the agent to explore futures that remain insufficiently organized in the learned representation. To incorporate information about physical dynamics, we additionally modulate this reward using bounded multi-step Hamiltonian variation, rather than directly rewarding changes in the Hamiltonian itself. We integrate HTC$^2$ with both Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), and evaluate it across six DeepMind Control Suite tasks. Comparisons with ICM, RIDE, E3B, Plan2Explore, and a single-step Hamiltonian curiosity baseline are complemented by state-coverage evaluations, component ablations, and phase-space diagnostics to characterize the contributions of temporal learning and physical structure to exploratory behavior.

physical.title: Labference: Benchmarking the Reasoning-Action Connection in Robotic Laboratories
physical.summary: Realizing Embodied AI for Science requires robots to translate experimental goals into reliable physical procedures, reducing hazardous and repetitive human work while generating evidence for scientific discovery. Although language-based planning and learned manipulation provide complementary capabilities, their integration requires robots to adapt subsequent operations to actual execution outcomes. For example, an unsuccessful placement changes what must be done next, even when the experimental goal remains unchanged. Existing benchmarks assess planning, manipulation, and laboratory workflows through task completion and reasoning or execution metrics; however, aggregate performance leaves the connection between outcome-dependent choices and physical execution unresolved. To address this evaluation gap, we introduce Labference, a benchmark for evaluating how observed physical outcomes guide subsequent choices and how those choices translate into robotic laboratory actions. Its evaluation protocol is designed to test outcome-dependent behavioral adaptation through controlled evidence variations, while independently measuring operation selection, physical execution, and task completion. Matched Oracle-assisted continuations from shared checkpoints then assess which forms of support improve subsequent choices and task completion. Initial weighing evaluations reveal target-selection errors in the tested VLA policies despite successful object transfers, whereas GPT-driven control achieves correct selection but encounters execution failures and substantial computation costs. Together, these findings highlight the need to connect task-appropriate reasoning with reliable, timely action. By making this connection measurable and diagnosable, Labference supports targeted improvements toward autonomous experimentation for Embodied AI for Science.

physical.title: PushAround: Collaborative Path Clearing via Physics-Informed Hybrid Search
physical.summary: Large vehicles in cluttered environments are often blocked by movable obstacles, motivating mobile robot teams to clear traversable corridors. Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) approaches often abstract obstacle displacements while neglecting robot dimensions, obstacle mass, contact geometry and forces, yielding physically infeasible plans. PushAround is a physics-informed hybrid search that couples geometric connectivity reasoning with short-horizon simulation to construct executable clearing plans. Repeated W-clearance connectivity graph (WCCG) queries expose frontier gaps requiring widening and rank them by estimated downstream costs. The search generates direct or recursive pushing candidates, selecting obstacles, directions, contacts and forces, and admits physics-evaluated candidates. Numerical experiments validate WCCG against standard connectivity checks and demonstrate scaling to denser clutter and teams of up to four robots, with robustness to simulated execution-side physical-parameter mismatch.

physical.title: How Much Sensing is Enough? Landslide Detection from Sparse and Noisy 3D Observations
physical.summary: Dense 3D terrain information is critical for accurate landslide detection; however, acquiring such data at large scale is often limited by sensing infrastructure, coverage, and environmental conditions. Emerging sensing modalities (e.g., mmWave, low-cost radar, sparse LiDAR) can operate under adverse conditions, but inherently produce sparse and noisy 3D observations, raising an important question: \emph{how much sensing is sufficient for reliable landslide detection?} Given the absence of large-scale sparse-terrain datasets, we have constructed a physics-informed dataset by combining digital elevation models from OpenTopography with soil moisture data from NASA's SMAP. Subsequently, we have randomly generated landslide events and introduced controlled sparsification and stochastic noise to emulate sensing constraints. We have then developed a learning-based framework to reconstruct the underlying terrain and identify landslide-prone regions using a CNN + XGBoost method. Our results show that with only 20\% of the original observations, the proposed method achieves a detection accuracy of 80\% and a ROC-AUC of 0.868, with a reconstruction error (L2 Chamfer Distance) of 99.67~$m^2$ on the test set. We have further studied the impact of sparsity, highlighting the trade-off between sensing density and detection performance.

physical.title: Physics-Informed and Data-Driven Composite Disturbance Separation and Predictive Control for Airborne Electro-Optical Gimbals with Multiple Constraints
physical.summary: This paper studies the constrained pointing control problem of airborne electro-optical gimbals subjected to composite periodic and aperiodic disturbances. Under carrier vibration, input delay, and actuator constraints, achieving line-of-sight stabilization and tracking is challenging. A disturbance-separated model predictive control (MPC) scheme is proposed to compensate these heterogeneous disturbances according to their physical characteristics. An adaptive periodic observer predicts multi-harmonic vibrations over the MPC horizon using linear-regression frequency estimation. A linear observer estimates the aperiodic disturbance, and a bounded long short-term memory (LSTM) network predicts its change over the input delay. Embedding periodic predictions into the MPC model while applying aperiodic compensation outside the optimizer limits amplification of aperiodic estimation errors and improves pointing accuracy under frequency changes and parameter mismatch. On the stated headroom envelope, input-set tightening provides feasible commands within the prescribed limits, and a regional practical tracking bound is established under explicit input-sequence and predicted-state margin conditions. A UAV-mounted two-axis gimbal platform is assembled for comparative indoor hovering experiments, complemented by simulations under frequency changes and parameter mismatch. In the reported trials, the proposed method achieves yaw and pitch relative-angle root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 0.770 degrees and 0.350 degrees, reducing tracking errors by 25.1% and 45.9% compared with linear active disturbance rejection control.

physical.title: Behavioural Quality Is Not Learning Utility: Objective Mismatch in Human Behaviour Models for Robot Learning
physical.summary: Human behaviour models are increasingly used to provide simulated human interactions for training robots via reinforcement learning (RL). Existing approaches primarily evaluate these models according to how closely their generated behaviours resemble real human data, while their usefulness as training partners is less commonly assessed. This creates a potential objective mismatch: a model that performs well according to behavioural evaluation metrics may not necessarily provide useful training experiences for downstream robot policy learning. Across two human-robot interaction (HRI) domains, highway driving and object handover, we evaluate different types of human behaviour models using common generative-model evaluation metrics. We consider multiple human trajectory representations and compare the resulting evaluations with the downstream performance of RL policies trained using the corresponding models. We find that existing behavioural evaluation metrics do not consistently predict downstream policy performance across domains and trajectory representations, while their evaluations are sensitive to the choice of trajectory representation. We also show that even when the true testing behaviour distribution is known, training against a different distribution may yield better downstream performance than training directly against the true distribution.

physical.title: Beyond Behaviour: A Stimulus-Response Safety Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Models
physical.summary: Humans exhibit biological sensitivity to safety-critical stimuli that can trigger defensive action. Across three models and two video benchmarks, we investigate whether similar responses emerge in vision-language-action models by examining their internal representations and action tendencies in response to visible hazards and harmful consequences. Our findings suggest that task execution may remain the default response even when danger is internally registered.

physical.title: AuRA: From Atoms to Bits through Autonomous Robot Interaction
physical.summary: Simulation enables robot-learning experiments at scale, but acquiring physics-informed digital twins often requires human manipulation and manual annotation of recorded interactions. To reduce this reliance on human effort, we present AuRA, a system that automates robot interaction and data preparation for digital-twin reconstruction. AuRA combines execution-aware grasp selection, gripper-motion measurements derived from robot states, and registered pre-interaction geometry and appearance priors. These choices enable autonomous collection, avoid reliance on visual gripper tracking, and recover object information obscured by the robot. Across 13 deformable objects, AuRA reduces active human labor and wall-clock collection time per successfully reconstructed asset by 88.5% and 55.4%, respectively. Relative to the human-collected PhysTwin baseline, AuRA improves seven of nine metrics for future prediction under known gripper motion, including a 28.1% reduction in one-way $L_1$ Chamfer distance. It also achieves similar mean silhouette IoU and Chamfer distance under the evaluated unseen interactions. These results highlight the potential of autonomous robot interaction to support more efficient digital-twin acquisition with comparable reconstruction quality.

physical.title: EAST: Embodied AI Safety Testing via Systematic Fault Injection in Digital Twins
physical.summary: Task success is not a sufficient measure of safety for embodied artificial intelligence (AI), because robots may complete objectives while violating safety requirements. Existing evaluations often emphasize performance and robustness, but lack a systematic route from documented safety hazards to executable, verifiable tests. We present EAST (Embodied AI Safety Testing), a digital-twin framework that converts literature-grounded safety evidence into fault-injection tests across perception, instructions, environments, actions, and timing. EAST combines an expert-reviewed safety-fault taxonomy and eight executable operators with applicability and validity constraints. Its three-stage workflow generates test specifications, verifies fault realization during simulated execution, and independently assesses safety challenges, violations, task outcomes, and behavioral signatures using simulator-state evidence. The framework preserves execution traces and replayable records, supporting attribution and reproducibility across experiments. We evaluate EAST on six RoboTwin manipulation tasks and two policy architectures, ACT and RDT, against alternative testing strategies under matched budgets. Across five comparative campaigns, EAST targets all 74 admissible task-policy-operator combinations and obtains valid evidence for 63, while achieving safety-challenge exposure rates close to Random-Legal and Rule-Based. Moreover, 82 valid EAST executions complete their tasks despite safety violations, revealing risks concealed by success-oriented evaluation. These findings support systematic, validity-aware, reproducible safety testing beyond task-completion metrics.

physical.title: Lie Symmetry-Guided Adaptive Sampling for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
physical.summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising mesh-free framework for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), with broad applications in physics, engineering, and medicine. However, their performance is highly sensitive to the sampling strategy for training points. Conventional uniform sampling often fails to adequately resolve regions with complex solution features, leading to low efficiency and limited accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose a Lie symmetry-driven adaptive sampling framework for PINNs, termed Lie-AS-ISC. For PDEs admitting Lie symmetry groups, symmetry transformations are exploited to derive intrinsic functional relationships between the solution and its variables, enabling the construction of basis points with exact solutions that span the solution domain. Building on this, an adaptive sampling strategy is developed by jointly considering absolute error and invariant surface conditions, while a dual-index loss is introduced to enhance training constraints. The proposed method significantly improves prediction accuracy. The experimental results show that this method consistently outperforms existing methods in accuracy.

physical.title: Self-Supervised Passive WiFi CSI-Based Motion Tracking with Physics-Informed Deep SSM
physical.summary: Inferring target position from WiFi channel state information (CSI) is challenging due to the noisy and heterogeneous nature of CSI-derived observations. Measurements such as angle, delay, and Doppler provide only imperfect information about target position and velocity, particularly in dynamic multipath environments where observation reliability varies. Motivated by this challenge, this paper proposes a physics-informed Bayesian state space framework for passive CSI-based tracking. We introduce a context-conditioned deep state space model (DSSM) that captures temporal motion and environmental dynamics, while adaptively modeling time-varying observation uncertainties. By incorporating geometric constraints, this framework enables heterogeneous CSI measurement modalities to jointly regularize the consistency and confidence of the tracking process. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework yields smoother trajectory estimates with reduced temporal fluctuations and outperforms existing methods in tracking accuracy.

physical.title: The Symmetry of Differential Neural Tangent Kernel under the Orthogonal Group
physical.summary: The differential neural tangent kernel (DNTK) is a tool for analyzing the training dynamics of overparameterized physics informed neural networks. In this work, we investigate the symmetry of the infinite DNTK under an orthogonal group, for two layer and deep neural networks separately, based on the explicit expression of the DNTK and recursive formula, respectively. The results are for all activations with or without a bias term, and shed insight into the structure of the infinite width DNTK. Then we prove that the integral operators over the unit sphere induced by operators from the same group orbit share the spectrum, and their reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces differ only by an orthogonal transformation, and that the operator fixed DNTK exhibits zonal symmetry on the unit sphere for symmetric operators. Thus the eigenvalue decay rate of the associated integral operator can be derived for shallow networks with RePU activation and zero bias initialization.

physical.title: Deep Scientific Reasoning under Physical Constraints: Structure-Aware Spectrum Prediction
physical.summary: Structured scientific spectra encode rich physical information while obeying hard constraints, such as conservation laws and characteristic spectral geometry. Accurate prediction of these spectra is central to materials discovery, yet existing methods often treat them as unconstrained sequences and therefore fail to enforce the underlying physical structure. Taking electronic density of states (eDOS) as the prototypical example, we introduce DeepSciReasoner, a general paradigm for predicting scientific spectra under physical constraints. The framework combines structure-aware spectrum decoding with constraint-preserving physical reasoning, allowing predictions to capture rich spectral structure while respecting the underlying physics. We evaluate DeepSciReasoner on eDOS, phonon density of states (phDOS), X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), and Raman spectra, where it substantially improves prediction accuracy while maintaining physical consistency. These results establish DeepSciReasoner as a reusable blueprint for structured scientific spectrum prediction under hard physical constraints.

physical.title: Securing Edge & Physical AI: Post-Quantum IoT Blockchain for Mission-Critical Cyber-Physical Agents
physical.summary: Distributed Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and Edge AI networks increasingly depend on public-key authentication and key-establishment mechanisms that are vulnerable to cryptographically relevant Quantum Computers (QC). Shor's algorithm threatens widely deployed asymmetric primitives, while Grover's algorithm reduces the effective security margins of symmetric and hash-based mechanisms. Although Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) provides a migration path, its larger public keys, ciphertexts, and signatures introduce additional computation, memory, communication, storage, and packet-fragmentation costs that can constrain dynamic multi-agent systems. In this article, we introduce rotational secrecy, an architectural objective that limits temporal key exposure through authenticated transitions between cryptographic epochs.
